intro.title: Explore Centro Histórico de Évora
intro.description: Welcome to the Centro Histórico de Évora, widely known as the Historic Centre of Évora - the UNESCO-listed heart of the city of Évora, the historic capital of Portugal's Alentejo region. The old town sits on the gentle hills of the Alentejo and is enclosed by medieval walls, earning it the title of an open-air museum. Over two thousand years of civilization converge here, preserving ancient Roman ruins, Moorish alleys, Gothic churches and Renaissance civil architecture. The old town is centred around Praça do Giraldo, with narrow ancient alleys radiating outward. Jardim Diana stands on the high ground of the old town, linking the Roman Temple of Évora with the episcopal complex. Whitewashed walls with wrought-iron balconies and hand-painted azulejo tiles form the iconic streetscape. From the centre, visitors can easily walk between the landmark monuments of Évora - the Roman Temple of Évora, the Sé de Évora cathedral, the Chapel of Bones and the Água de Prata aqueduct - which are described in detail below.

visitGuide.title: Visiting Tips
items: The city features many uneven cobblestone streets; non-slip, comfortable walking shoes are essential. Most guesthouses within the old town can assist with short-distance luggage transfers.
Summer daytime temperatures are high. Ensure adequate sun protection, carry drinking water, and avoid the midday heat.
Tour groups mostly arrive at popular sites in the morning. For a quieter experience, try to enter as soon as the venues open.
Local public museums offer free admission on Sundays; religious sites are not included in this offer.

alsoKnownAs.title: Attraction Highlights
items: Multi-Era Monument Clusters: the 1st-century AD Roman Temple of Évora, the medieval Sé cathedral, the 16th-century Chapel of Bones and Renaissance noble mansions are concentrated within one small centre.
Authentic Medieval Streets: Moorish-style winding cobblestone paths lined with whitewashed houses and hand-painted azulejo tiles.
Panoramic Viewpoints: the cathedral roof terrace and Jardim Diana offer sweeping views over the red-tiled roofs of the old town and the surrounding Alentejo plains.
Living Local Culture: squares surrounded by open-air cafés and artisan shops, blending historic monuments with everyday Alentejo life.

knowledge.title: Discover the Charm of Centro Histórico de Évora

sections.title: History
sections.content: Évora's history spans over two thousand years. Known as Ebora Liberalitas Julia in Roman times, the town flourished under Muslim rule and was taken by Geraldo Sem Pavor (Gerald the Fearless) in 1165, becoming one of the most important cities of the young kingdom of Portugal. Its historic centre preserves this layered past - Roman foundations, medieval streets, Gothic churches and Renaissance palaces. In 1986 the Historic Centre of Évora was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List (reference 361).

sections.title: Architecture & Views
sections.content: The historic centre is defined by its medieval walls, winding alleys, whitewashed houses and azulejo-tiled facades. Its outstanding monuments span two millennia: the Roman Temple of Évora, the Romanesque-Gothic Sé cathedral, the Gothic and Manueline Igreja de São Francisco, Renaissance palaces and the 16th-century Água de Prata aqueduct. The ensemble is often described as a museum-city of Portuguese architecture.

sections.title: Core Experience
sections.content: Start at Praça do Giraldo, follow the alleys up to the Sé de Évora and its roof terrace, then descend to the Chapel of Bones, Jardim Diana and the Roman Temple of Évora. In the evening the temple is illuminated and the old town remains lively with cafés and restaurants - the perfect way to end a day in Évora.

hours.title: Opening Hours
hours.outdoorTime: The old town streets, Praça do Giraldo, and Jardim Diana are open 24/7 for free. Paid indoor venues have seasonal scheduled opening hours.
hours.summerTime: Regularly 9:00-17:00, slight adjustments on public holidays
hours.warningTime: Outdoor ruins open 24/7, attached small exhibition hall has limited hours
hours.tip: Best visited from April to October (Spring to Autumn); July and August are very hot at noon, so early morning or evening is preferred.

tickets.title: Ticket Information
tickets.outdoor: Old Town Public Streets, Plazas, Temple Exteriors
tickets.childrenPrice: Motor vehicles are prohibited inside the ancient walls. Several free public parking lots are available just outside the walls, requiring only a 5 to 10-minute walk into the old town.
tickets.cardPrice: Discounted combo tickets available for multiple venues

transport.title: Transportation
transport.airportDesc: Nearest international airports: Lisbon (LIS) Airport (approx. 135 km, 1h 25m drive) and Faro (FAO) Airport (approx. 240 km, 2h 50m drive). Renting a car upon arrival is recommended.
transport.selfDriveDesc: From Lisbon, take the A2 highway south, then connect to the A6 directly to Évora. Navigate to Jardim Diana and park in the lots outside the city walls.
transport.busDesc: Take a Rede Expressos intercity bus from Sete Rios station in Lisbon directly to the Évora bus station, which is within walking distance of the old town. Alternatively, there are direct trains from central Lisbon to Évora, requiring a short walk into the city.
transport.intercityDesc: The old town is entirely navigable on foot. The surrounding suburban plains are flat and ideal for cycling or chartering a car to visit nearby megalithic monuments and wineries.
transport.cyclingDesc: The surrounding Alentejo region and Alqueva reservoir offer relatively flat and scenic routes, perfect for both road and mountain biking.
transport.tipsDesc: Due to limited public transport schedules in the Alentejo region, renting a car is strongly advised for the flexibility to explore nearby wineries, megalithic monuments, and the Alqueva Dam.

route.title: Visiting Route
steps: Walk from the outside parking lot through the ancient aqueduct gate into the old town
Explore Praça do Giraldo and take a short break
Walk to visit the Church of St. Francis and the Chapel of Bones
Head to the Évora Cathedral and climb to the terrace for a panoramic view
Move to Jardim Diana to view the Roman Temple from a distance
Get up close to the remaining columns of the Roman Temple of Diana
Wander through the old town alleys in the evening and taste local specialties
supplements: Cobblestone streets can be slippery; wear comfortable, non-slip shoes.
Dining options are limited; booking in advance during peak season is advised.
Summer midday sun is intense; stay hydrated and use sun protection.

spots.name: Niche Cobblestone Alleys in the West

hotels.title: Accommodation Suggestions

hotels.name: Historic Guesthouses Inside the Walls
hotels.desc: Converted from old noble mansions, steps away from major monuments.
hotels.price: Advance booking required in peak season

hotels.name: Suburban Estate Hotels
hotels.desc: Converted old monasteries and rural farms, often featuring courtyard pools.

hotels.name: Budget Apartments Outside the Old Town
hotels.desc: Close to parking lots with plenty of dining options nearby.

hotels.supplementsContent: Focuses on rustic Alentejo cuisine: bread soup, garlic braised dishes, regional wines, and traditional Portuguese sweets. Local flavor restaurants are scattered throughout the old town alleys, perfect for spontaneous dining.

items.name: João Silva
items.text: A beautifully preserved historic centre. The Roman Temple above Jardim Diana is stunning, and walking the old streets around Praça do Giraldo feels like stepping back in time.

items.name: Maria Costa
items.text: One of my favourite towns in Portugal. The view from the cathedral terrace over the rooftops and the Alentejo plains is unforgettable. Go early in summer to avoid the midday heat.

items.name: Carlos Rodrigues
items.text: Perfect for a day trip from Lisbon. The Chapel of Bones is unique and the old town is full of character. Parking can be tricky in summer, so arrive early.

items.name: Ana Martins
items.text: Spent a full day here without getting bored - Roman temple, cathedral, museum and cafés in the old streets. Very walkable and full of history at every corner.

items.name: Pedro Santos
items.text: Two thousand years of history in one small centre is remarkable. The illuminated Roman Temple at night is beautiful and great for photos.

items.name: Teresa Ferreira
items.text: Easy train ride from Lisbon. Wear comfortable shoes for the cobblestones and save time for the cathedral terrace - the view is the highlight.

items.name: Rui Almeida
items.text: A must-see in the Alentejo. Strolling through the alleys, watching the sunset from Jardim Diana and tasting the local food made it a perfect day.

items.name: Catarina Gomes
items.text: Compact but rich - Roman ruins, Gothic cathedral, bone chapel and whitewashed alleys. The best part is the atmosphere of the old town at dusk.

officialManagement.title: About Centro Histórico de Évora
officialManagement.text: The Centro Histórico de Évora is the UNESCO World Heritage old town of Évora, capital of Portugal’s Alentejo region (inscribed in 1986, ref. 361). This website is an independent visitor guide and has no official affiliation; for authoritative information always consult the Câmara Municipal de Évora and the Direção-Geral do Património Cultural.

thingsToSee.title: What to See & Visit in Évora
thingsToSee.subtitle: The must-see sights of the UNESCO Historic Centre of Évora, all within easy walking distance of each other.

items.name: Roman Temple of Évora (Templo Romano)
items.desc: The best-preserved Roman temple in Portugal, standing on granite Corinthian columns above Jardim Diana since the 1st century AD - one of the symbols of the city.

items.name: Sé de Évora (Évora Cathedral)
items.desc: Begun in 1186, this Romanesque-Gothic cathedral rises over the old town. Climb to the roof terrace for panoramic views of the Alentejo plains.

items.name: Chapel of Bones & Igreja de São Francisco
items.desc: A 16th-century Franciscan church whose famous Chapel of Bones is lined with thousands of human bones and skulls - an unforgettable sight.

items.name: Praça do Giraldo
items.desc: Évora's historic main square and the lively heart of the old town, with its Renaissance fountain and the Church of Santo Antão.

items.name: Aqueduto da Água de Prata
items.desc: A Renaissance aqueduct commissioned by King João III (1531-1537); its arches cross the fields and pass through the old town walls.

items.name: University of Évora
items.desc: A Jesuit university founded in 1559; its arcaded cloisters decorated with blue-and-white azulejos form one of the most elegant corners of the city.

items.name: Museu Nacional Frei Manuel do Cenáculo
items.desc: A national museum housed in the archbishop’s palace beside the Roman Temple, displaying Roman archaeology and European painting.

items.name: City Walls & Gates
items.desc: The medieval walls and gates that still encircle the centre shape its UNESCO-protected character; views from the walls stretch over the surrounding plains.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Practical answers about visiting the Historic Centre of Évora.

items.q: Where is the Historic Centre of Évora located?
items.a: The Centro Histórico de Évora is the walled old town of Évora, the main city of the Alentejo region in Portugal. The main access is through Praça do Giraldo, while Jardim Diana and the Roman Temple of Évora stand on the highest ground of the old town. Address: Jardim Diana, 7000-661 Évora, Portugal. See the exact location on the map below.

items.q: What can you visit and see in Évora in one day?
items.a: A day is enough to walk the compact historic centre and see its main landmarks - the Roman Temple of Évora, the Sé de Évora cathedral and its roof terrace, the Chapel of Bones, Praça do Giraldo, the University of Évora and the Água de Prata aqueduct. Start with the list of what to visit in Évora and follow the suggested walking route.

items.q: Is the Historic Centre of Évora free to visit?
items.a: The outdoor area of the historic centre - streets, squares and the exterior of the monuments - is open to the public 24 hours a day and free to visit. The Roman Temple stands in the open air. Indoor monuments such as the Chapel of Bones, the cathedral museum and the viewing terrace charge admission; see the opening hours section for details.

items.q: How much time do you need to visit the historic centre of Évora?
items.a: Allow 3-4 hours for a relaxed walk covering the main sights: the Roman Temple, the cathedral roof terrace and the Chapel of Bones, with a coffee break at Praça do Giraldo. With a full day you can also visit the museums, the University of Évora and the Almendres Cromlech on the outskirts.

items.q: How do you get from Lisbon to Évora?
items.a: By car it is about 135 km via the A2/A6 motorways (around 1h30). By train, Comboios de Portugal (CP) runs regular services from Lisbon to the Évora station, about a 15-minute walk from the old town. Rede Expressos buses also connect Lisbon (Sete Rios) to the Évora bus terminal near the centre.

items.q: Where can you park to visit the historic centre of Évora?
items.a: Motor traffic is restricted inside the walls. Use the car parks located just outside the old town and walk in 5-10 minutes. In summer, arrive early as spaces fill quickly.

items.q: When is the best time to visit the historic centre of Évora?
items.a: April-October (spring to autumn) offers the best conditions. July and August can be very hot at midday, so plan your walk for the early morning or the late afternoon; summer evenings are particularly pleasant.

items.q: Is the Historic Centre of Évora a UNESCO World Heritage site?
items.a: Yes. The Historic Centre of Évora was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986 (reference 361) as an outstanding example of a Renaissance city adapted to its medieval and Roman roots.

facilities.title: Practical Facilities & Services
facilities.subtitle: Useful amenities for exploring the Historic Centre of Évora.
facilities.note: This is an independent, non-profit educational website. We list facility types only, in a neutral way, and do not recommend any specific business or brand; always confirm exact locations on site or on a map.

items.name: Public Toilets
items.desc: Public toilets are available near the main squares and sights of the old town; some require a small fee. Many cafés and museums also offer facilities to visitors.

items.name: Parking (outside the walls)
items.desc: Motor traffic is restricted inside the walls. Paid and free car parks sit within a 5-10 minute walk of the old town; in peak season spaces fill early, so arrive early or use public transport.

items.name: Restaurants & Cafés
items.desc: The old town is dense with restaurants, small taverns (tasca), cafés and pastry shops, from quick snacks to full meals.

items.name: Hotels & Guesthouses
items.desc: Inside the walls you will mostly find small boutique hotels, guesthouses (alojamento local) and family-run lodgings within walking distance of the sights; more options exist just outside.

items.name: Supermarkets & Shops
items.desc: Small supermarkets, grocery stores, bakeries and souvenir shops are scattered through the old town for daily needs, drinks and snacks.

items.name: Fuel & EV Charging
items.desc: Petrol stations and electric-vehicle chargers are located mainly on the ring roads outside the walls; drivers are advised to refuel or recharge before entering the old town.

items.name: Banks & ATMs
items.desc: Bank branches and cash machines (ATMs) are found near the main streets and squares of the old town; most accept international cards.

items.name: Pharmacies & Health
items.desc: Évora has several pharmacies and primary-care points; for emergencies or a full hospital, head to the municipal hospital outside the walls.

stories.title: Stories, History & Legends
stories.subtitle: Key moments and tales from over two thousand years of Évora - every account below is based on documented history and chronicles.

items.title: 1165: Geraldo Sem Pavor and the city that joined Portugal
items.content: Évora had flourished under the Romans and again under Muslim rule, but during the Portuguese Reconquista this still Moorish-held city was taken in 1165 by the knight Geraldo Sem Pavor ('Geraldo the Fearless'). The town was quickly rebuilt, work on its cathedral began in 1186, and Évora became a lasting part of Portugal - a key stronghold in King Afonso Henriques' expansion to the south.

items.title: How did Geraldo get in? Firewood carts or a herd of oxen
items.content: Accounts of the 1165 conquest differ: some say Geraldo's soldiers slipped into the city hidden among carts of firewood, others that Christians inside opened the gates while the garrison relaxed during Holy Week (Semana Santa). The details are hard to prove, yet chronicles and local memory have retold them ever since, adding legend to the 'Fearless' knight. Whatever truly happened, September 1165 was a turning point for Évora.

items.title: The misnamed temple: the Diana mystery
items.content: The Roman temple that crowns the hill above the old town was once buried inside medieval castle and town-hall structures and only freed again in the 19th century. In the 16th century the humanist André de Resende first called it the "Temple of Diana", and the beautiful mistake stuck. Modern scholars lean towards an imperial cult or Jupiter, but the true deity remains unproven - which only adds to its mystery.

items.title: The Chapel of Bones: meditating among skeletons
items.content: In the 16th century, Franciscan monks lined the walls of a side chapel at São Francisco with thousands of bones gathered from nearby cemeteries, as a reminder of life's brevity. Above the entrance still stands the famous Portuguese motto: 'Nós ossos que aqui estamos, pelos vossos esperamos' - 'We bones that are here, await yours'. It may be Europe's most striking epitaph.

items.title: A university with two lives: 1559 and 1973
items.content: In 1559 Cardinal-King D. Henrique founded a Jesuit university in Évora, making it one of Portugal’s centres of learning. In 1759 the Marquis of Pombal expelled the Jesuits and the university closed. Only in 1973, after a gap of more than two centuries, did the University of Évora reopen on the same site - its azulejo-lined arcaded cloisters still tell the story of an ending and a rebirth.

items.title: The Água de Prata aqueduct and the homes between its arches
items.content: Between 1531 and 1537 King João III commissioned the architect Francisco de Arruda to build the aqueduct that brought spring water into the town. Explanations for the name "Água de Prata" (silver water) vary - some say the water gleamed like silver, others link it to how the works were financed. Most curious of all, houses were later built between the arches, creating streets where home and aqueduct merge; they can still be seen along the old walls today.

items.title: 1663: the year Évora was lost and regained
items.content: During the Portuguese Restoration War, Spanish troops briefly occupied Évora in May 1663. A month later the Portuguese army won the Battle of Ameixial and forced the occupiers to withdraw, returning Évora to Portugal. The episode is a reminder that this quiet historic centre was once a prize fought over by crowns.
